artboards.title: Review queue — the screen, Cross-references tab
The same screen, the other two tabs
A · Evidence beside decision — CHOSEN, built
B · Dense triage — explored, not chosen

annotations.text:
WHAT THIS BOARD IS
One screen: the review queue, where a person answers the questions the system could not answer by itself. A single design, already built — nothing here is asking you to choose between options.

The board to the right is the SAME screen with the other two tabs selected, so you can see one example of each review type.

WHO IT IS FOR
A contracts or procurement specialist. They know what a schedule and a defined term are. They have never seen a file path or a confidence score, and they should need no training to start.

WHAT CHANGED THIS ROUND
· One review type at a time. Tabs across the top carry the pending count for each, and picking one makes the whole page that type — so it is never unclear which kind of judgement is being asked for.
· Much less text. The question and the answers are what stay on screen; the reasoning moved behind "Why am I being asked?" and the guidance behind "How to decide", both closed by default.
· The unresolved cross-reference no longer reads as an error. It now asks you to confirm the target, so the link connects by itself when that schedule is loaded.

WHAT I WOULD VALUE YOUR EYES ON
1. Is one type at a time the right call, or would you rather see the mix?
2. Is there still a sentence on screen that is not pulling its weight?

ABOUT THE PAGE IMAGES
The grey blocks standing in for page crops are placeholders, drawn here rather than pasted. The running app cuts the real image out of the PDF when the row loads.

One caveat that is expected for now: the fixture coordinates are invented, so a crop in the running app shows real ink from the real page but not the sentence beside it. That resolves itself the moment real pipeline output replaces the fixtures.

ON THE VISUAL STYLING
Now built in the Whitespace product register from the brand memo: a neutral near-black ground, cards a step up from it, one flat action blue for anything you can act on, Inter for text and JetBrains Mono for references and page numbers. Status is a small pill, never a wash across a row.

The marketing lavender and the gradient appear only where the memo allows them: the soft glow in the corner behind the composer, and the connectors on the connections view. Nothing else borrows from the marketing look.

British English throughout, sentence case on product labels.

HOW WE GOT HERE — reference only, no decision needed.

Before building, three directions were sketched for a single review row. A was chosen and is what page 1 shows.

WHY A: the queue exists to turn a reviewer's judgement into ground truth, so a verdict reached without looking at the page is worse than no verdict at all — A is the only one that makes the page image impossible to skip, and keyboard triage buys back the density it costs.

B stays the right answer once the system has earned trust and volume dominates. C is the arbitration view for a single contested item. Both are kept here so the reasoning stays visible; neither needs your approval.
